diagram_name: Which Lesson Does the Failure Teach?
chapter_title: AI-First Case Studies II: Lessons for Practice
learning_objective: The learner will classify seven real failures as teaching one of seven lessons, correctly matching at least six of seven on the first attempt.
specification:
Type: microsim **sim-id:** which-lesson-does-failure-teach
**Library:** p5.js
**Status:** Specified
**Bloom Level:** Understand
**Bloom Verb:** classify
**Learning Objective:** The learner will classify seven real failures as teaching one of seven lessons, correctly matching at least six of seven on the first attempt. **Prerequisites:** the seven cases and their lessons (all described in the section "When Technology Came First" above). **Evidence of Mastery:** The learner places each of 7 failures in one of seven lesson bins and submits it. A placement is correct when it matches the "Correct lesson" column in Content. Mastery is 6 of 7 correct on the first attempt. Reading the case summaries is exploration, not evidence. **Misconceptions:** (1) All the failures show the same mistake. (2) Technology failures are caused by weak technology. (3) A data failure is a security failure only. **Instructional Rationale:** Matching each failure to the lesson it teaches requires understanding the cause, not just the name. Cases that look alike, such as the two Los Angeles programs, make the learner separate planning from vendor choice. **Content:** Seven lessons, shown as bins. The labels L1 to L7 are for this specification only; the learner sees each lesson's short form. | Lesson | Short form | |---|---| | L1 | Plan the teaching before buying devices | | L2 | Set procurement rules and check a vendor's survival | | L3 | Technology without a lasting culture does not last | | L4 | Listen to students about screens and contact with teachers | | L5 | Earn family trust and make data ownership clear | | L6 | Centralized records are a large target; hold less | | L7 | Redesign assessment instead of relying on detectors | Seven failures: | # | Failure shown to the learner | Correct lesson | Why (shown as feedback) | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | A district announced a \$1.3 billion plan to give every student an iPad, and cancelled it amid technical problems and weak curriculum. | L1 | The devices came before the teaching plan. | | 2 | A district committed about \$6 million to an AI chatbot startup that collapsed within months. | L2 | There were no procurement rules or checks on the vendor's survival. | | 3 | A well-funded network of personalized microschools closed its schools within a few years and sold its software instead. | L3 | The technology had no lasting culture around it. | | 4 | Students walked out and families protested over long screen hours and too little contact with teachers. | L4 | Students and families were saying what was not working. | | 5 | A state-spanning student data project closed after parents objected over privacy. | L5 | Families did not trust a central store, and ownership was unclear. | | 6 | A breach at one student information vendor exposed records of tens of millions of students and teachers. | L6 | Holding very many records in one place created a very large target. | | 7 | Popular AI-writing detectors wrongly flagged essays by non-native English writers. | L7 | Detectors produce false and biased accusations; redesign the assessment. | **Provenance:** The cases and lessons come from the book's AI-First Stories appendix and Chapters 10, 20, and 21, and the sim must say "Check figures against the sources." The lessons' short forms are this book's wording. **Rules:** Each failure has exactly one correct lesson, given in Content, and each lesson has exactly one failure. A failure is scored on its first submitted placement only. The score counts first-attempt correct placements out of 7. Mastery is a score >= 6. **Learner Activity:** 1. The learner sees one failure at a time and the seven lessons. 2. The learner places the failure and submits it. The sim marks it correct or incorrect and shows the feedback text. 3. If incorrect, the learner may place it again; the second attempt does not change the score. After the second attempt, the correct lesson and reason are shown. 4. After all 7 failures, the sim shows the score and the pairs. 5. The learner should notice that each failure matches a practice from an earlier chapter. **Feedback:** 7 failures, shuffled once per session, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: [lesson]. [Why text]." Incorrect: "Not quite. Ask what caused the failure. [Why text for the correct answer, without naming the lesson]." After the second attempt the correct lesson is revealed and the failure counts as missed. A running score "First-try correct: n of 7" is shown. Final message for a score >= 6: "You can say what each failure teaches." For a score < 6: "Review the seven cases and try again; the failures will be reshuffled." **Starting State:** Failure 1 of the shuffled order is shown with the seven lessons, the score "First-try correct: 0 of 7," and the prompt "Which lesson does this failure teach?" **Chapter Anchors:** The chapter's table pairs the iPad rollout, the Ed chatbot, AltSchool, the Summit walkouts, inBloom, the PowerSchool breach, and the AI detectors with the seven lessons in that order. The mastery bar is 6 of 7.
